rationale: I own three shares of Accenture, bought nine days ago at $251.845 and now marked at $237.85, down 5.56%. That tells me nothing about the business, and a price decline of that size is no reason to sell. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 26.9%, debt-to-equity of 0.32, and owner earnings averaging about $9.26 billion against a $143 billion market cap. The model's intrinsic value of $437.57 gives a 46.6% margin of safety, but I would not lean on it: it rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and the snapshot doesn't say what the 5% discount rate is built from. My real worry is whether AI erodes the moat of a consulting and outsourcing firm, and I can't verify client retention or pricing power from these numbers. So I keep what I own and don't add until I'm surer the moat isn't being rebuilt every year.

rationale: I own this one, a small position bought two days ago, and the question is whether to keep it, not whether to open it. Best Buy sells televisions, laptops and appliances through big stores and a website, a business I understand, but the moat is thin: scale buying power and service, up against Amazon and the manufacturers. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 48.35% and debt-to-equity of 0.37, and the price sits about 15.3% below my owner-earnings value of $117.52, just clearing the 15% bar. But that value assumes zero growth and a 5% discount rate, and the snapshot gives me no ten-year earnings record, so I cannot check the consistency test. I will hold the shares, not add to them, and I will sell only if the moat or management actually deteriorates, not because the price wiggles.

rationale: I don't own Adobe, and the numbers in front of me are striking: a 5-year average ROE of 40.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.41, and a price of $232.95 against a computed intrinsic value of $467.50. I can see the switching costs, since designers and studios build their workflows around these tools, but I can't tell you with confidence that the moat won't have to be rebuilt continuously. I'll keep this on the list and wait until I can answer the durability question, rather than buy it on the strength of a spreadsheet.

rationale: I own General Dynamics, so the question is whether to keep it, and I'm keeping it. It builds nuclear submarines, combat vehicles and Gulfstream jets, and the submarine franchise sits behind a wall of security clearances, specialized shipyards and a single customer that has few alternatives. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 17.2% and debt-to-equity of 0.30, both inside my thresholds, and a margin of safety of 15.1% against an owner-earnings DCF value of about $417 per share. That clears my 15% bar only by a hair, and the DCF leans on an 8% growth cap and a 5% discount rate, so I'm not adding much on that cushion. I bought at $353.20 and the shares are at $354.32, a gain of 0.32% in 28 days. That tells me nothing either way, and I'm not selling a decent franchise because of 28 days. Several checks I would want, such as ten years of earnings, CEO tenure and the history of capital allocation, are not in this snapshot. I can't confirm them from what I was given, so my confidence stays moderate.
